spec.prompt:
ROLE: librarian

You are the librarian of a team attacking the problem in `problem.md`. You
prove nothing. Your job is to find the literature the team should read before
planning, so that the planners and provers are not limited to the few papers
in `papers/`.

## Task

1. Read `problem.md` and the papers in `papers/`, in particular their
   reference lists: the works they cite are the best leads.
2. Search the web for further relevant works: journal articles, books,
   preprints, theses, survey articles, lecture notes and blog posts. Useful
   topics include, for example, squarefree and k-free numbers in arithmetic
   progressions, the Barban–Davenport–Halberstam and Montgomery–Hooley
   theorems and their variants, variances over sparse sets of moduli,
   exponential sums over k-free numbers, and the distribution of polynomial
   values modulo q. Follow citations in both directions.
3. For each work, find its exact bibliographic data and check, by opening it,
   whether its full text is openly available as a PDF: an author's home page,
   arXiv, an institutional repository, a journal's open-access page. Never
   use shadow libraries (Sci-Hub, LibGen, Anna's Archive, Z-Library and the
   like) or unauthorised copies.

## What to list

- Only works published, or posted as a preprint, **in 2010 or earlier**
  (rule 4 below). A work you only know from a later citation is fine if the
  work itself is from 2010 or earlier.
- Nothing by the excluded author, and not the excluded paper (rule 1 below).
- Not the papers already in `papers/`.
- Aim for 10–30 works, the most useful first. A short list of works that
  matter beats a long list of works that only share keywords.

## Fields

- `id`: a short key such as `croft1975`.
- `authors`, `title`, `year`, `venue` (journal with volume and pages,
  publisher, or "preprint"), `kind`.
- `url`: the landing page (journal page, DOI link, MathSciNet or zbMATH entry,
  arXiv abstract page).
- `pdf_url`: only a direct link to the full text as a PDF that you have
  checked is openly available. Leave it out if you are not sure; a wrong
  `pdf_url` wastes a download, a missing one only costs a manual look.
- `access`: `open` if `pdf_url` is set, `paywalled` if the full text is
  behind a paywall, `unknown` otherwise.
- `relevance`: 3 = likely needed for the proof, 2 = useful background or
  method, 1 = related.
- `why`: one or two sentences on what the work contains that the team would
  use, e.g. which lemma or estimate.

Use `notes` for anything else the team should know, such as a gap in the
literature or a key work you could not identify exactly.


## Rules for every agent on this project

1. **Excluded author.** Markus Schepke (who also publishes as Markus Shepherd)
   wrote a master's thesis on exactly this problem. The point of this project is
   to solve it independently of that work. Do not search for, open, fetch or
   read anything written by him: his thesis, his blog (riemannhypothesis.blog,
   primes.recommend.games, mshepherd.gitlab.io), his GitLab projects, or any
   other source by him. If a search result or a source turns out to be his,
   stop, use nothing from it, and say so explicitly in your output. The same
   applies to anything you may remember about his work: do not use it.
   **Excluded paper.** The same rules apply to Fabian Dehnert, *Sparse variance
   for k-free numbers in arithmetic progressions*, Monatsh. Math. 177 (2015),
   373–396 (doi:10.1007/s00605-014-0691-6), which solves this problem too: do
   not search for, open or use it, or anything you remember of it.
2. Work only with the files in your current directory and with the published
   literature. Do not read or list files outside your current directory.
3. Cite every external source you use: authors, title, year, and URL or arXiv
   id.
4. **Literature up to 2010.** Use only literature published, or posted as a
   preprint, in 2010 or earlier, plus the papers in `papers/` (Brüdern–Wooley
   2011 among them). This applies to searching, reading and citing, and to
   results you remember: do not use a result first published in 2011 or
   later, even if you know it. If a source turns out to be from 2011 or later,
   stop reading it, use nothing from it, and say so in your output.
5. **Python.** If you can run commands, `python3` has numpy, scipy, mpmath
   and sympy installed, besides the standard library; use them as you like.
   Installing anything else is not possible in your sandbox, so don't try.
6. **Reading PDFs.** Poppler's `pdfinfo`, `pdftotext` and `pdftoppm` should
   be available to you. Use `pdftotext -layout` to extract text and, when
   supported, render relevant pages with `pdftoppm` to check equations,
   tables or unclear extraction visually. You are free to use a different
   tool if it works better for you. If Poppler is unavailable, flag this to
   the user for installation; do not try to install it in your sandbox.
   Keep any extracted text or rendered pages within your current directory.

leak_patterns: distribution of squarefree numbers in arithmetic progressions

items.title: On a variance associated with the distribution of general sequences in arithmetic progressions. II
items.venue: Phil. Trans. R. Soc. Lond. A 356 (1998), no. 1738, 793–809
items.why: This is ref. [7] of Vaughan 2005. It gives Montgomery–Hooley-type asymptotics for general sequences that are approximately distributed in every residue class, not only the reduced ones, which is the situation for squarefree numbers. Its Theorem 1.2 and hypothesis (1.12) are what Vaughan 2005 sharpens. It is the template for the 'classical' route, with error at least x^{1+1/k} log x, and for the structure of the main term x^2 F(x/Q).

items.title: On a variance associated with the distribution of general sequences in arithmetic progressions. I
items.venue: Phil. Trans. R. Soc. Lond. A 356 (1998), no. 1738, 781–791
items.why: This is ref. [10] of Brüdern–Wooley. It is the circle-method treatment of the Montgomery–Hooley variance for general sequences equidistributed in reduced classes. Brüdern–Wooley say their major-arc treatment, with auxiliary averages of multiplicative functions, mirrors this paper.

items.authors: D. A. Goldston and R. C. Vaughan
items.title: On the Montgomery–Hooley asymptotic formula
items.venue: Sieve Methods, Exponential Sums, and their Applications in Number Theory (Cardiff, 1995), LMS Lecture Note Ser. 237, Cambridge Univ. Press (1997), 117–142
items.why: Origin of the method: the variance is reduced to counting n1 − n2 = hq with q ≤ Q and evaluated by the circle method, the minor arcs being handled through the product hq. Brüdern–Wooley adapt exactly this to n1 − n2 = h f(k). Page 118 has historical comments on the method. The DOI in the URL was not verified; check the landing page.

items.title: On a variance associated with the distribution of primes in arithmetic progressions
items.why: Ref. [11] of Brüdern–Wooley. A refined circle-method analysis of the prime variance with an explicit secondary main term. It is useful for how to extract the lower-order main terms from major arcs and singular-series-type averages.

items.authors: H. Mikawa and T. P. Peneva
items.title: Primes in arithmetic progressions to spaced moduli
items.why: The Barban–Davenport–Halberstam upper bound for primes with moduli f(k), weighted by f'(k) or k^{-1}φ(f(k)). This is the sparse-moduli predecessor that Brüdern–Wooley sharpen to an asymptotic, and a model for the upper-bound (BDH) part of the squarefree problem.

items.title: Square-free numbers in arithmetic progressions
items.why: First BDH/Montgomery–Hooley-type result for squarefree numbers, summing over all residue classes mod q (not only coprime ones), as in the present problem. Caution: Vaughan 2005 (p. 574) says the argument leading to Croft's (6.6) is faulty and the constant B in his (7.2) is wrong. Use it for structure only, not for constants.

items.title: Squarefree numbers in arithmetic progressions
items.why: Gives V(x,Q) = x^2 F(x/Q) + O(x^{3/2}(log x)^{7/2}) for squarefree numbers with F(y) = c y^{-3/2} + O(...), avoiding Croft's error. This is the classical benchmark main term c x^{1/2} Q^{3/2} for all moduli, against which the sparse main term should be checked.

items.title: On squarefree numbers in arithmetic progressions
items.why: Early variance and BDH-type bounds for squarefree numbers in progressions; cited by both Vaughan 2005 and BGPVW. The DOI was not verified; check via EuDML/GDZ, where Monatshefte scans of this era are often freely available.

items.title: Über quadratfreie Zahlen in arithmetischen Progressionen
items.why: A short follow-up improving the squarefree variance bounds; ref. [9] of Vaughan 2005.

items.title: Remainder estimates for squarefree integers in arithmetic progression
items.why: Mean-square and individual remainder estimates for Q(x;q,l) (from Orr's 1969 Syracuse thesis under Richert). Halberstam remarked that it is hard to improve upon. A source of elementary bounds for E(x;q,l) uniform in q and l. The DOI was not verified; older JNT volumes are in Elsevier's open archive.

items.title: A note on square-free numbers in arithmetic progressions
items.why: An individual bound for E(x;q,l), improving Prachar, which gives an asymptotic for Q(x;q,l) for q up to about x^{2/3−ε}. Useful for disposing of moduli f(k) in ranges where pointwise bounds suffice, and for the trivial estimate of the variance.

items.title: Über die kleinste quadratfreie Zahl einer arithmetischen Reihe
items.why: The classical elementary asymptotic Q(x;q,l) = g(q,l)x + O(x^{1/2}q^{-1/4}+q^{1/2+ε}) type for squarefree numbers in a progression. It is the simplest pointwise input. EuDML lists the full text via the Göttingen digitisation centre (GDZ).

items.title: On the frequency of pairs of square-free numbers with a given difference
items.why: An asymptotic for Σ_{n≤x} μ²(n)μ²(n+h) with explicit dependence on h. Expanding V_f gives correlations Σ μ²(n)μ²(n+h f(k)), and the elementary (non-circle-method) route needs exactly such shifted-pair sums with error uniform in the shift. The AMS PDF is at ams.org/bull/1949-55-10/S0002-9904-1949-09313-8; AMS back issues are normally free, but the fetch was blocked so access was not verified.

items.title: Note on an asymptotic formula connected with r-free integers
items.why: Asymptotics for Σ μ_r(n+k_1)…μ_r(n+k_s) (r-free tuples) with error x^{2/(r+1)+ε}; cited by BGPVW. A k-free analogue of the shifted-correlation input. The DOI was not verified.

items.title: The square sieve and consecutive square-free numbers
items.why: Improves the error term for Σ μ²(n)μ²(n+1) to x^{7/11+ε} via the square sieve. Relevant if the team uses correlations of μ² with shifts; it shows the limits of the elementary error term. EuDML (doc 163852) lists it, likely with GDZ full text.

items.authors: J. Brüdern, A. Perelli and T. D. Wooley
items.title: Twins of k-free numbers and their exponential sum
items.why: L1 and L2 bounds for exponential sums over k-free twins, extending BGPVW's estimates for Σ μ_k(n)e(nα). Useful for minor-arc and mean-value bounds involving μ². Wooley's site lists a copy (math.purdue.edu/~twooley/publ/2000ktwin.pdf), but the fetch failed, so it is not verified. The page range is from memory: the search snippet showed 173–177, which looks truncated, so verify it.

items.title: Goldbach numbers in sparse sequences
items.why: Ref. [1] of Brüdern–Wooley: a circle-method treatment of additive problems along sparse sequences, including polynomial-value-type sets. Brüdern–Wooley borrow from it for handling sums over f(k) on major and minor arcs. The open Numdam/Centre Mersenne PDF was confirmed as a 1.6 MB AIF 48(2) p. 353 file.

items.title: On the Barban–Davenport–Halberstam theorem. I
items.why: Hooley's refinement of Montgomery's asymptotic, V(x,Q) = Qx log Q + cQx + O(...), via an elementary divisor-switching method. It is the classical alternative to the circle method and the source of the second main term. EuDML links the full text at GDZ (free), but it was not downloaded.

items.title: On the Barban–Davenport–Halberstam theorem. II
items.why: Ref. [6] of Brüdern–Wooley: further refinement of the Montgomery–Hooley formula, including what happens when the residue-class sum is over all classes. Background only.

items.title: Primes in arithmetic progressions
items.why: The original asymptotic for the BDH variance of primes, by expanding the square and counting n1 ≡ n2 mod q. Gives the basic expansion that all later works follow. Michigan Math. J. is free on Project Euclid, but the PDF could not be fetched to confirm.

items.authors: J. B. Friedlander and D. A. Goldston
items.title: Variance of distribution of primes in residue classes
items.why: Variance for a single modulus q near x, with the explicit correction term; cited by Brüdern–Wooley. Background on behaviour when moduli are large relative to x (the range f(y) close to x).

items.title: Bombieri–Vinogradov type theorems for sparse sets of moduli
items.why: BV and BDH-type theorems for sparse sets of moduli, e.g. squares and polynomial values, via large sieve inequalities for sparse moduli. An alternative (large-sieve) route to the upper bound for V_f, and a source of the admissible range of f(y) relative to x.

items.title: An improvement for the large sieve for square moduli
items.why: A large sieve inequality Σ_{q≤Q} Σ_{a mod q²} |Σ a_n e(an/q²)|² with improved bounds. Relevant if the team bounds V_f(x,y) from above by a large sieve with polynomial moduli (squarefree indicator as the sequence).

items.title: The large sieve with sparse sets of moduli
items.venue: J. Ramanujan Math. Soc. 21 (2006) (venue from memory, unverified); preprint arXiv:math/0508417 (2005)
items.why: A general large sieve for sparse moduli that are well distributed in progressions (extending Wolke), applied to squares. Gives a general framework for moduli f(k).

items.title: On the distribution of the roots of polynomial congruences
items.why: Equidistribution of ν/n for roots ν of f(ν) ≡ 0 mod n, via exponential sums over roots. Needed when counting k ≤ y with f(k) ≡ 0 mod d (or f(k) in a class) with error terms uniform in d, as in the main-term evaluation Σ_k f'(k)·(arithmetic function of f(k)). The DOI was not verified.

items.title: On the number of solutions of polynomial congruences and Thue equations
items.why: Sharp uniform upper bounds for ρ(p^k), the number of roots of f mod p^k, in terms of degree and discriminant. These are needed to control ρ(m) and the multiplicative functions built from it on all prime powers, including primes dividing the discriminant. AMS JAMS back content is usually free, and a scan is hosted at uwaterloo.ca/pure-mathematics (s0894-0347-1991-1119199-x_0.pdf), but its content could not be confirmed by text extraction.

items.title: A note on polynomial congruences
items.venue: Recent Progress in Analytic Number Theory, Vol. 1 (Durham, 1979), H. Halberstam and C. Hooley (eds.), Academic Press, London (1981), 193–196
items.why: Bound ρ(p^k) ≤ d·p^{k/2}-type, more precisely in terms of the discriminant, for the number of roots of f mod p^k. A simpler alternative to Stewart for showing ρ is O(m^ε) and multiplicative sums over ρ converge.

items.title: Short sums of certain arithmetic functions
items.why: Upper bounds of the expected order for Σ_{k≤y} F(|f(k)|) with F submultiplicative, e.g. divisor functions of polynomial values. Handy for bounding error terms like Σ_k τ(f(k)) that arise when E(x;f(k),l) is estimated pointwise. Acta Math. is now open on Project Euclid (euclid.acta/1485891131), but the PDF could not be fetched to confirm.

items.title: On the sum Σ_{k=1}^x d(f(k))
items.why: Σ_{k≤x} d(f(k)) ≍ x log x for irreducible f. The elementary prototype for the divisor-of-polynomial-value bounds needed in error terms. The DOI was not verified.

items.title: The Hardy–Littlewood Method, 2nd edition
items.venue: Cambridge Tracts in Mathematics 125, Cambridge University Press (1997)
items.why: Standard reference cited by all three corpus papers: Weyl's inequality, major-arc approximations, and the complete exponential sums S(q,a) = Σ e(a f(x)/q) bounds (Hua) needed for sums over k of e(α h f(k)) on the minor arcs.

items.authors: E. C. Titchmarsh (revised by D. R. Heath-Brown)
items.title: The Theory of the Riemann Zeta-Function, 2nd edition
items.why: Vaughan 2005 uses §6.19 (Vinogradov–Korobov zero-free region and bound for 1/ζ) and §§3.12–3.13 for Lemma 2.1 (Σ_{n≤y,(n,q)=1} μ(n)) and for the exp(−c(log x)^{3/5}(log log x)^{−1/5}) error terms.

items.authors: H. L. Montgomery and R. C. Vaughan
items.title: Multiplicative Number Theory I. Classical Theory
items.venue: Cambridge Studies in Advanced Mathematics 97, Cambridge University Press (2007)
items.why: Background on Dirichlet series of multiplicative functions, Perron's formula and contour shifting. This is the technique for evaluating the auxiliary sums Σ_q h(q)·(stuff) whose generating function involves ζ(2s+…) as in Vaughan 2005 §6.

output.notes:
I found no source by the excluded author (Markus Schepke / Markus Shepherd), and none of his sites (riemannhypothesis.blog, primes.recommend.games, mshepherd.gitlab.io) came up. Nothing by or about the excluded Dehnert paper was searched for or opened.

Post-2010 works seen only as search-result titles or snippets, not opened and not used: Nunes (arXiv 1402.0684, 2014), Le Boudec (2015–16), Gorodetsky–Matomäki–Radziwiłł–Rodgers (arXiv 2006.04060, 2020), R. C. Baker "Primes in arithmetic progressions to spaced moduli" I–III (2012–2017), Brüdern–Wooley "Sparser variance for primes in arithmetic progression" (arXiv 1706.07319, 2017), Vaughan's arXiv survey "The generalized Montgomery–Hooley formula" (arXiv 2605.18996, 2026), Harper (2024), and Baier–Pujahari (2023). Snippet details from these (e.g. Hooley 1975's range x^{2/3−ε}, Croft's main result) are used in the 'why' fields above; check them against the originals.

Key points for planners:
(1) Vaughan 2005 relies on Vaughan 1998 Part II (pp. 793–809, general sequences in all residue classes), not Part I. Brüdern–Wooley rely on Part I (pp. 781–791) and Goldston–Vaughan 1997. Both parts are needed.
(2) Vaughan 2005 (p. 574) says Croft 1975 is faulty at (6.6) and its constant is wrong. Warlimont 1980 gives the correct classical squarefree result.
(3) The main-term evaluation will need averages over k ≤ y of f'(k) times multiplicative functions of f(k) (or of gcds with f(k)). This means counting k with d | f(k), i.e. ρ(d), uniformly in d. I found no pre-2010 paper doing exactly this for the squarefree variance with polynomial moduli. Brüdern–Wooley §§5–6 (primes) is the closest model, and the literature on ρ (Hooley 1964, Huxley 1981, Stewart 1991, Nagell's classical bound for p ∤ disc) supplies the inputs.
(4) Mirsky 1949 (shifted squarefree pairs) is the natural input for an elementary route that expands the square and counts n1 − n2 = h f(k).

Access caveats:
- A scan of Vaughan 1998 Part I sits on a Williams College course-handout page. Its authorisation is unclear, so I did not list it.
- Royal Society, Project Euclid, AMS and zbMATH pages returned 403 or empty to my fetcher, so several likely-free items (Montgomery 1970, Mirsky 1949, Stewart 1991, Nair–Tenenbaum 1998, Hooley BDH I via GDZ) are marked 'unknown' rather than 'open'.
- An unofficial Springer mirror (elogim.com) appeared for Heath-Brown 1984; I did not use it.

Items not fully identified:
- Baier, 'The large sieve with sparse sets of moduli': the journal reference (J. Ramanujan Math. Soc. 21, 2006) is from memory. arXiv lists no journal reference.
- Several DOIs are from memory or pattern and were not opened: Goldston–Vaughan, Warlimont 1969, Orr, Mirsky 1947, Hooley 1964, Erdős 1952. Each is noted in its 'why' field; check them.
